b.bio: Quodvultdeus was a fifth-century bishop of Carthage. He appears first as a deacon corresponding with Augustine of Hippo in 428–429, asking him for a book on heresies; Augustine answered with his De haeresibus and dedicated other writings to him. Sources place his accession to the see of Carthage in 432 or 433. When Gaiseric's Vandals took the city in 439, he was exiled by ship to Naples, where he spent the rest of his life; Victor of Vita records the expulsion. His death is variously given as about 450, 453, or shortly before October 454, when Deogratias succeeded him.
b.s: The letters held here show him as Augustine's correspondent on method in cataloguing heresies—weighing Philastrius against Epiphanius and pressing the reply to Julian of Eclanum over new composition.

b.bio: Quintianus of Asculum is not the same person as the better-attested Quintian of Rodez and Clermont (d. c. 525), a Latin bishop from Africa; surviving records describe that Gaulish saint and say nothing about an Asculum bishop, so they are set aside. What is known comes from the library's own holding: four pages in Migne's Patrologia Graeca 85 preserving a short polemical work under his name as Bishop of Asculum.
b.s: The single surviving piece is a compact Chalcedonian polemic: it argues for two natures in Christ united indivisibly, against Theopaschites and Eutychians/Miaphysites, with side references to Arius, Manichaeus, Valentinus, and Eutyches.
